title: How Mechanisms Work: What Happens When This Turns?
description: Rotation goes in; something surprising comes out. A differential lets two wheels turn at different speeds while both are driven, a Geneva drive turns smooth rotation into precise stops, and a sewing machine ties a knot with a thread that never passes through the fabric. Predict what each mechanism does, then watch it move.

questions.title: A car's differential drives both rear wheels from one input shaft. What actually lets the outer wheel spin faster than the inner wheel when the car turns a corner?

images.alt: Two-panel schematic of an open differential. Left panel, driving straight: a ring gear (marked driven) turns a carrier holding two small spider gears, which mesh with two side gears connected to equal-length axle shafts, and both wheels show equal-length speed arrows. Right panel, turning a corner: the same gear set now shows the inner wheel's speed arrow shorter than the outer wheel's.

options.text: Small spider (pinion) gears inside the carrier roll around their own axles, redistributing rotation between the two side gears while both keep receiving torque
A centrifugal clutch in the carrier disengages whichever wheel is turning faster
The outer wheel's half-shaft is slightly longer and twists elastically to absorb the speed difference
A ratchet inside the hub lets the outer wheel freewheel ahead of the drive

questions.explanation: A differential is a small epicyclic gear train. The ring gear turns a carrier; mounted on that carrier are one or more spider (pinion) gears that mesh with two side gears, one bolted to each half-shaft. Driving straight, both wheels need to turn at the same speed, so the spider gears don't spin on their own pins — they just orbit with the carrier, and both side gears turn at carrier speed. In a turn, the outer wheel has to cover a longer arc than the inner one in the same time. The spider gears start rotating on their own axles, letting one side gear speed up exactly as much as the other slows down, while the carrier keeps turning at the average of the two. No clutch, no twisting shaft, and no ratchet is involved: the freedom comes entirely from that extra degree of rotation the spider gears have around their own pins — the same gear geometry used in a planetary gear set.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Differential (mechanical device)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_(mechanical_device)) · [tec-science: How does a differential gear work?](https://www.tec-science.com/mechanical-power-transmission/planetary-gear/how-does-a-differential-gear-work/)

questions.title: One rear wheel of a car sits on dry pavement; the other sits on ice. With a normal open differential, what happens when the driver presses the accelerator?

images.alt: Two-panel schematic of an open differential. Left panel, driving straight: a ring gear (marked driven) turns a carrier holding two small spider gears, which mesh with two side gears connected to equal-length axle shafts, and both wheels show equal-length speed arrows. Right panel, turning a corner: the same gear set now shows the inner wheel's speed arrow shorter than the outer wheel's.

options.text: Almost all the torque goes to the wheel on ice, because a differential always sends equal torque to both side gears, and the icy wheel only needs a tiny amount of torque to spin freely
Torque splits evenly and both wheels push the car forward with equal effectiveness
The differential senses reduced traction and automatically routes more torque to the wheel with grip
The differential locks solid the instant it detects a speed difference, so neither wheel can turn

questions.explanation: An open differential does not choose the wheel with grip — it does the opposite, and that is the counterintuitive part. The spider gears inside the carrier always push on both side gears with equal torque at every instant; that equal push is also what lets the two side gears spin at different speeds. Once the wheel on ice starts to slip, it takes almost no torque to keep it spinning, so that becomes the torque the whole differential settles into transmitting through both sides. The wheel with grip, which could actually move the car, receives exactly as little torque as the slipping wheel needs. This is why a single spinning wheel can strand a car even though the other wheel has traction, and it is exactly the failure that a limited-slip or locking differential is built to resist by forcing torque toward the wheel that can use it.

questions.title: In a standard lockstitch sewing machine, the needle carries a thread down through the fabric on every stitch. Where does that needle thread actually lock together with the bobbin thread?

images.alt: Three-panel schematic of one lockstitch cycle: the needle descends through the fabric; the needle rises slightly and leaves a loop, which a rotary hook below enters; the hook carries the loop in a full circle around the bobbin case, and the interlock forms inside the fabric layers.

options.text: It never crosses to the other side — a rotary hook catches a small loop left by the needle and carries it fully around the bobbin case, so the two threads interlock inside the layers of fabric
It passes all the way through the fabric and is tied to the bobbin thread on the underside, visible from below
It wraps around the bobbin thread on top of the fabric, and both threads are then pulled down together
It never interacts with the bobbin thread at all; the bobbin thread only holds the fabric layers together on its own

questions.explanation: This is the part almost nobody predicts correctly: the needle thread never travels through to the far side of the fabric. As the needle rises slightly after piercing the fabric, it leaves a small loop of thread behind it. A rotary hook, spinning at twice needle speed, catches that loop with its point and carries it in a full circle around the bobbin case, looping the needle thread completely around the bobbin thread. Both threads are then pulled taut so the interlock — the 'lock' in lockstitch — settles inside the fabric, roughly midway between its two faces, instead of sitting on the underside. That is also why a correctly formed lockstitch looks identical from the top and the bottom, and why cutting that buried interlock partway through a seam lets the whole line of stitching pull apart.

questions.title: A Geneva drive takes a continuously spinning input wheel and uses it to move a second, driven wheel. What does that driven wheel actually do?

images.alt: Three-panel schematic of a Geneva drive across one cycle. A driving wheel carries a single pin and a raised locking disc and turns continuously beneath a slotted driven wheel. Panel one: the pin is outside any slot and the locking disc holds the driven wheel still. Panel two: the pin has entered a slot and the driven wheel is stepping around. Panel three: the pin has left the slot and the locking disc holds the driven wheel still again, now in a new position.

options.text: It rotates in short, equal steps with a full stop between each one, even though the input wheel never stops turning
It rotates at a constant fraction of the input's speed, simply geared down
It oscillates back and forth instead of continuing to rotate in one direction
It spins in brief fast bursts with no pause, momentarily matching the input's speed during each burst

questions.explanation: A Geneva drive, also called a Geneva mechanism or Maltese cross mechanism, converts continuous rotation into intermittent rotation with genuine full stops. The driving wheel carries a single pin and a raised locking disc that covers most of its circumference. As the pin sweeps into one of the driven wheel's radial slots, it pushes that wheel through a fixed angle — one step — while the locking disc is briefly clear. The instant the pin exits the slot, the locking disc immediately re-engages a matching concave edge on the driven wheel and holds it perfectly still until the pin comes back around for the next slot. The driven wheel is at rest for most of each cycle and moving only briefly, which is exactly the motion a film projector needs to hold one frame still in the gate before snapping to the next — this intermittent 'movement' is a standard part of classic film projector design — and clocks and watch complications use the identical trick to advance a wheel by one indexed count per cycle.

questions.title: A worm (a screw-shaped shaft) drives a toothed worm wheel. Why can you usually turn the worm to lift a heavy load, but you cannot turn the worm wheel backward to lower that load by pushing on it?

images.alt: Side-view schematic of a worm meshing with a worm wheel: the worm is drawn as a shaft with a shallow helical thread, marked driven, engaging the teeth around the rim of a large worm wheel.

options.text: The worm's thread is wound at such a shallow angle that friction between the thread and the wheel's teeth resists the sliding needed to back-drive the worm from the load side
A separate ratchet pawl physically blocks the worm wheel from rotating backward
The worm wheel's teeth are cut with a reversed pitch that only accepts motion from one direction
An electric brake automatically engages whenever load is applied to the worm wheel

questions.explanation: It comes down to the worm's lead angle — how steeply its thread winds, like the pitch of a screw. Driving the worm wheel from the load side tries to spin the worm around its own axis, but that requires the contact point between thread and tooth to slide along a very shallow helix, and friction at that shallow angle resists the sliding more than the small mechanical advantage available in that direction can overcome. Turning the worm itself slides the same contact point along the tooth in the direction friction does not oppose, so it drives the wheel normally. Whether a given worm gear is self-locking this way depends on its lead angle and the friction between the materials: shallow leads with ordinary friction lock, while steep leads or very low-friction coatings can be back-driven. This is exactly why worm gears show up in hoists, jacks, and tuning pegs — the load cannot spin the mechanism back on its own, so no separate brake is needed to hold position.
questions.references: [tec-science: How does a worm drive work?](https://www.tec-science.com/mechanical-power-transmission/worm-gear/self-locking-worm-gear/) · [Wikipedia: Worm drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worm_drive)

questions.title: A single universal (Cardan) joint connects two shafts that meet at an angle. The input shaft spins at a perfectly constant speed. Which of these are true of the output shaft's speed?
questions.description: Select every statement that is true.

images.alt: Schematic of a single universal joint: a straight input shaft, marked driven, connects through a cross-shaped pivot to an output shaft angled downward away from the input shaft's line, with the angle between the two shafts marked.

options.text: It speeds up and slows down twice during every single revolution of the input shaft
The size of that speed swing grows as the angle between the two shafts increases
Using two universal joints in series, correctly phased, can cancel the speed variation so the final output shaft turns at a constant speed
The output shaft's average speed over a full revolution ends up different from the input shaft's speed

questions.explanation: A single universal joint cannot transmit constant velocity through an angle, no matter how precisely it is built — this is a geometric limitation, not a manufacturing defect. As the cross rotates through the angled joint, the effective radius it acts through keeps changing, so the output shaft alternately runs ahead of and behind the input, completing two full speed-up-and-slow-down cycles per revolution. The larger the angle between the shafts, the larger that oscillation becomes. Over one complete revolution the speed-ups and slow-downs cancel out, so the average speed still matches the input exactly — it is only the instant-to-instant speed that wobbles, and that wobble is what causes vibration and extra wear at higher angles or higher speeds. The practical fix used in vehicle driveshafts is to place two universal joints in series with their yokes phased so the second joint's speed-up cancels the first joint's slow-down; a constant-velocity (CV) joint achieves the same constant output speed inside a single joint using an entirely different internal geometry.

questions.title: A mechanical clock stores energy in a wound spring or a falling weight. What does the escapement actually do with that stored energy?

images.alt: Three-panel schematic of an escapement cycle: a toothed escape wheel, marked driven, is alternately caught and released by two pallets mounted on a swinging arm, advancing by one tooth per swing as the arm moves from the left pallet catching, to the wheel briefly advancing, to the right pallet catching.

options.text: It releases the gear train forward by exactly one tooth at a time, in step with a swinging pendulum or balance wheel, turning continuously stored energy into equal, counted beats
It converts the spring's energy directly into the visual motion of the hands, with no other gearing involved
It stores the spring's energy a second time so the clock can keep running after the spring fully unwinds
It smooths the gear train's motion into continuous rotation, which is why a well-made clock produces no ticking sound

questions.explanation: The gear train under spring or weight power wants to unwind all at once, and the escapement is what stops it from doing that. An escape wheel, the last gear in that train, has teeth shaped to catch against two pallets mounted on an arm connected to the pendulum or balance wheel. As the pendulum swings one way, one pallet releases a tooth and lets the wheel advance slightly before the other pallet catches the next tooth; the swing back releases the following tooth the same way. Each release also gives the pendulum a small push, keeping it swinging against friction and air resistance. The result is that continuously stored energy gets metered out in equal, counted steps timed by the pendulum's own natural swing rate — the escapement is simultaneously a brake, a counter, and the thing keeping the pendulum going, and the audible tick is literally the sound of one tooth being caught.

questions.title: A pin tumbler lock has several spring-loaded pin stacks pressing down into the plug. What has to happen across all of those pin stacks at once before the correct key lets the plug rotate?

images.alt: Cross-section schematic of a pin tumbler lock: four pin stacks, each split into an orange key pin below and a blue driver pin above, sit in vertical chambers crossing the boundary between the fixed housing and the circular plug at different, mismatched heights; an arrow marks the plug as the part that turns once free to.

options.text: Every pin stack's split point, where key pin meets driver pin, must line up exactly at the boundary between the plug and the surrounding housing
The key must push every pin stack entirely out of the plug so that no pins remain inside it
The key must release a hidden magnetic catch that operates independently of the pins' heights
Only the single deepest pin stack needs to reach the correct height; the rest only add friction

questions.explanation: Each pin stack is really two pins — a key pin below and a driver pin above — pushed down by a spring, straddling the gap between the fixed housing and the rotating plug. With no key inserted, at least one driver pin sits across that gap and physically blocks the plug from turning. The correct key lifts every key pin to exactly the right height so that each pin stack's split point lands precisely at the boundary between plug and housing, all at the same time; the plug can then rotate freely because no single pin is left straddling the gap anywhere around the cylinder. A wrong key gets at least one pin stack's split point off that boundary, so a pin still crosses into the plug and binds against the housing the moment you try to turn it — it only takes one pin out of place to stop the whole lock. Picking a lock works by applying slight rotational tension and setting each pin at that boundary one at a time, exploiting tiny manufacturing tolerances that let one pin bind before the others do.

questions.title: A bicycle freewheel lets you stop pedaling while the bike keeps rolling, but pedaling still drives the rear wheel forward. What inside the freewheel makes both of those things true?

options.text: Spring-loaded pawls catch against the steep face of a ratchet ring's teeth when pedaling drives it forward, but simply ride up and over the same teeth's shallow face when the wheel overtakes the pedals
A centrifugal clutch disengages the pedals once the wheel's speed exceeds the pedaling speed
The chain itself goes slack and stops transmitting any force the moment you stop pedaling
A fluid coupling transmits force only in the forward direction and slips freely in reverse

questions.explanation: The mechanism is a ratchet and pawl. The ratchet ring's teeth are cut asymmetrically: one face of each tooth is steep, the other shallow. Spring-loaded pawls sit against the steep faces, so when the sprocket is driven forward by pedaling, a pawl catches a steep face almost immediately and locks the ratchet to the hub, transmitting torque to the wheel. When the wheel starts spinning faster than the pedals — coasting, or freewheeling while braking — the shallow faces of the same teeth slide underneath the pawls, camming them up and out of the way with a soft click each time, so the ratchet spins freely inside the hub. No clutch or fluid coupling is involved anywhere; the tooth shape alone decides which direction transmits force and which direction slips.

questions.title: In a typical piston engine, the piston moves in a straight line while the crankshaft turns in a circle. How does the piston's speed actually change over the course of one stroke?

options.text: The piston moves fastest somewhere around the middle of its stroke and comes to a complete stop at each end, and because the connecting rod's angle keeps changing, that motion is not a perfect sine wave
The piston moves at constant speed throughout the stroke, just like a fixed point on the crankshaft's rim
The piston moves fastest at the very top and bottom of its stroke and slowest in the middle
The piston's speed depends only on engine RPM and is the same at every point within the stroke

questions.explanation: A crank and slider — the piston, connecting rod, and crankshaft of a typical engine — must bring the piston to a dead stop at top dead centre and bottom dead centre, because that is where its direction of travel reverses; it then accelerates back up to its fastest point somewhere near the middle of the stroke. If the connecting rod were infinitely long, the piston's position over time would trace a perfect sine wave, the same motion a Scotch yoke produces exactly. Because real connecting rods are a finite length and swing side to side as the crank turns, the piston actually reaches its peak speed slightly before mid-stroke and its motion is a bit lopsided compared to a pure sine wave — a detail engine designers account for when balancing vibration. Run the same mechanism in reverse, pushing the piston instead of turning the crank, and it converts that straight-line force back into rotation — exactly how a steam engine uses expanding steam to turn a wheel.

questions.title: A rotating cam pushes a follower up and down as the cam spins at a constant speed. What actually determines the exact up-and-down motion the follower traces out?

images.alt: Three-panel schematic of a rotating egg-shaped cam, marked driven, shown at its low point, at a rising edge, and at its highest lobe, with a follower resting on the cam's surface at a different height in each panel.

options.text: The cam's outline, its radius at every angle, is the whole program — whatever shape is cut into the cam becomes the follower's motion, timing, dwell, and speed
The follower's motion is always a smooth sine wave regardless of the cam's shape, because the rotation driving it is smooth
The follower's speed is set entirely by the spring holding it against the cam, not by the cam's shape
A cam can only move a follower up and down at a constant rate; it can never pause the follower or speed it up

questions.explanation: A cam is essentially motion stored as a shape. At every angle of rotation, the distance from the cam's centre to its edge sets the follower's position at that instant; as the cam turns at a steady speed, that changing radius is played back over time like a program, whether the profile calls for a smooth rise, an abrupt lift, a long flat dwell where the follower does not move at all, or a sudden drop. This is exactly how mechanical camshafts control when and how far engine valves open, how old music boxes and player pianos read a pattern, and how a sewing machine's feed dog gets its combined up-down-and-forward path from a stacked pair of cams. Change the cam's outline and the motion changes completely without touching anything else in the mechanism — the shape is the instruction set.

questions.title: A rack and pinion converts a pinion gear's rotation into the rack's straight-line motion. If the pinion is made bigger (more teeth, larger radius) while its rotation speed stays the same, what happens to the rack?

options.text: The rack moves faster for the same pinion rotation speed, because each revolution now sweeps out a longer arc length at the pinion's larger radius
The rack moves slower, because a bigger pinion requires more torque to turn
The rack's speed stays exactly the same; only the force it can push with changes
The rack starts moving in the opposite direction

questions.explanation: A pinion's teeth are spaced along its pitch circle, and the rack's linear speed equals the pinion's angular speed multiplied by its pitch radius. Enlarge the pinion, and for the same rotational speed — say, one revolution per second — its pitch circle's circumference is longer, so more length of rack passes by in that revolution: the rack moves faster. That speed gain comes at the direct expense of force: the same input torque, spread over a longer effective lever arm, pushes the rack with proportionally less force, the same trade every gear ratio makes between speed and force. This is why steering racks, rack-and-pinion elevator systems, and cog railways all choose pinion size deliberately, balancing how fast something needs to move against how hard the mechanism needs to push.

questions.title: A Scotch yoke converts a crank's rotation into straight-line motion using a pin that slides inside a slotted yoke. How does the yoke's back-and-forth motion compare to an ordinary crank-and-connecting-rod mechanism?

options.text: The Scotch yoke traces a mathematically pure sine wave, while a crank-and-rod's motion is only approximately sinusoidal because the rod's angle keeps changing
Both mechanisms produce an identical sine wave; the Scotch yoke is simply a cheaper way to build the same motion
The Scotch yoke moves in sudden jumps rather than continuous motion
The Scotch yoke can only complete part of a stroke and never finishes a full back-and-forth cycle

questions.explanation: In a Scotch yoke, the crank pin engages a slot cut perpendicular to the direction of travel, and that slot constrains the yoke's motion to be exactly the sine of the crank angle — pure simple harmonic motion, by construction. A crank-and-connecting-rod mechanism only approximates that same sine wave, and the approximation gets worse as the connecting rod gets shorter relative to the crank, because the rod's changing angle adds a distortion to the piston's motion that a Scotch yoke's slot never introduces. The tradeoff is friction and wear: the Scotch yoke's pin slides hard against the sides of its slot, especially near the ends of the stroke, while a connecting rod's joints mostly rotate rather than slide. That is why Scotch yokes show up where the pure sine motion matters more than mechanical efficiency, such as some control-valve actuators and quick-return machine tools, while engines almost always use a connecting rod instead.

questions.title: A four-bar linkage has four rigid links joined by four pivots. If the same four links stay the same length but a different one is fixed to the frame, what happens to the motion the linkage produces?

images.alt: Three-panel schematic of a four-bar linkage shown in three positions of its cycle. Each panel shows a fixed base link, marked driven at its left pivot, connected through two moving side links and a coupler link, with the coupler tracing out a curved path across positions.

options.text: The linkage can produce a completely different family of motion — for example switching from a link that spins fully around to one that only rocks back and forth — even though none of the link lengths changed
The motion is identical no matter which link is fixed, because the link lengths alone determine everything about the motion
Changing the fixed link only changes the linkage's speed, never the shape of the path any point on it traces
Fixing a different link to the frame is not physically possible once a four-bar linkage has been assembled

questions.explanation: The same four links, pin-jointed in the same loop, can behave completely differently depending on which one is bolted to the frame. With one link fixed, a four-bar linkage might become a crank-rocker, where one link spins continuously while the opposite one only rocks back and forth — the arrangement behind a sewing machine treadle or many windshield-wiper linkages. Fix a different link within that same four-bar chain and it might instead become a double-rocker, where nothing spins fully around, or a drag-link mechanism where both links touching the frame spin continuously at different, non-uniform rates. Because a point on the floating coupler link traces a distinctive curved path as the linkage moves, engineers also choose link lengths deliberately to make that coupler point draw a specific path — straight-line linkages like the Peaucellier–Lipkin mechanism exist for exactly that reason.

questions.title: A planetary gear set has a sun gear, several planet gears riding on a carrier, and a ring gear surrounding them. Which of these are true about driving it?
questions.description: Select every statement that is true.

images.alt: Schematic of a planetary gear set: a small central sun gear, marked driven, meshes with three planet gears linked together by a dashed carrier, which in turn mesh with a large ring gear surrounding the whole assembly.

options.text: The set has three members — sun, carrier, ring — and holding any one of them stationary while driving another produces a distinct fixed gear ratio out of the third
Locking any two of the three members rigidly together forces the entire gear set to rotate as one solid unit at a 1:1 ratio
Letting all three members rotate freely, with none held or locked, still delivers a single predictable output ratio
A planetary gear set can only produce gear reductions and can never produce a speed increase

questions.explanation: A planetary gear set has three members that can each act as an input, an output, or a held-still member, which is exactly what makes it so useful inside automatic transmissions and hub motors. Hold the ring gear and drive the sun, and the carrier comes out at one reduction ratio; hold the sun and drive the ring, and the carrier comes out at a different ratio; hold the carrier and drive the sun, and the ring turns at yet another ratio, sometimes in the opposite direction. Which member is held decides both the ratio and, in some combinations, whether the output reverses direction — and because the sun is usually smaller than the ring, some of these combinations are speed increases rather than reductions. Lock any two members rigidly together, though, and the third is forced to match them exactly, so the whole assembly can only turn as one solid piece at a 1:1 ratio — this is how automatic transmissions produce a direct-drive gear. With nothing held or locked, the set has too many degrees of freedom to give a single output: the sun, carrier, and ring can spin at three different, unrelated speeds simultaneously, which is exactly the extra freedom a differential — built from the same planetary geometry — relies on.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Epicyclic gearing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epicyclic_gearing) · [tec-science: How does a planetary gear work?](https://www.tec-science.com/mechanical-power-transmission/planetary-gear/planetary-gear-how-does-it-work/)

questions.title: A compound gear train uses several gears of different sizes meshed in sequence to connect a fast motor to a slow, high-torque output shaft. Which of these are true?
questions.description: Select every statement that is true.

options.text: As speed drops through each reduction stage, torque increases by roughly the same ratio, ignoring friction losses
Stacking several modest gear reductions in sequence can multiply into a very large overall ratio without needing one impractically large single gear
Every gear in the train, regardless of its size or position, carries the same amount of torque
The output's direction of rotation is guaranteed to match the input's direction, no matter how many gears are in the chain

questions.explanation: A gear train trades speed for torque at every meshing pair: power — roughly speed multiplied by torque — is conserved apart from friction losses, so wherever a smaller gear drives a larger one and speed drops, torque rises by close to the same factor. Chaining several such reductions multiplies their individual ratios together, which is how a compound train reaches enormous overall reductions, the kind used in a clock's minute-to-hour gearing or a hand winch, using several ordinary-sized gears instead of one gear with an impractical number of teeth. Because torque changes at every stage, the gears nearest the slow, high-torque output carry far more torque than the gears nearest the fast, low-torque motor, which is why those output-stage gears are usually built chunkier. And each individual meshing pair of external gears reverses rotation direction, so whether the final output spins the same way as the input depends on whether the chain has an odd or even number of meshing pairs.

questions.title: A bicycle rear derailleur moves the chain sideways between sprockets of different sizes. What actually forces the chain to climb from a smaller sprocket onto a larger one?

options.text: The derailleur's cage pushes the moving chain sideways just enough that, as it approaches the sprockets, it can no longer settle onto its old sprocket and instead rides up the guiding ramps machined into the larger one
The derailleur physically lifts the chain off the old sprocket and sets it down onto the new sprocket
A clutch inside the rear hub disengages the old sprocket, letting the chain fall onto the next one under gravity
The rider must stop pedaling completely before the chain is able to move sideways at all

questions.explanation: The derailleur never lifts or grabs the chain directly; all it does is deflect the moving chain sideways by a few millimetres just before it reaches the sprockets, using a spring-loaded parallelogram linkage and a small cage carrying two jockey wheels. Because the chain is still moving and under tension from pedaling, that small sideways offset is enough that the chain's rollers can no longer settle onto the teeth of the sprocket they were just riding. Modern sprockets are machined with subtle ramps and pins specifically shaped to catch a slightly offset chain and guide it up onto the next sprocket over roughly one pedal revolution. Because this shifting motion needs the chain actively moving through the derailleur under load, it only works while pedaling — which is also why shifting while coasting, or under very heavy pedaling force, tends to be rough or unreliable.

questions.title: A pulley-and-belt continuously variable transmission (CVT) changes its overall gear ratio smoothly instead of shifting between fixed steps. Which of these are true about how it does that?
questions.description: Select every statement that is true.

options.text: Each pulley is really two cone-shaped halves that can move closer together or farther apart, which changes the effective radius the belt rides at
Squeezing one pulley's halves together while the other's move apart shifts the belt to a different radius on each pulley at the same time, changing the ratio continuously
A CVT actually has a fixed, countable number of distinct gear ratios, just like a manual gearbox, but shifts between them faster
The belt's total physical length has to change as the ratio changes

questions.explanation: A belt-and-pulley CVT earns its 'continuously variable' name because it has no fixed steps at all — the ratio can sit anywhere within its range, not just at a countable set of gears. Both pulleys are actually two cone-shaped sheaves facing each other; moving them closer together forces the belt to ride higher up the cones, at a larger effective radius, while moving them apart lets the belt sink to a smaller radius. The two pulleys are always adjusted in opposite senses, one clamping in as the other opens up, because the belt's total length is fixed: the radius gained on one pulley has to be given up on the other. That constant back-and-forth adjustment of radius, not any discrete gear-swap, is what lets a CVT hold an engine near its most efficient RPM regardless of road speed, at the cost of a belt — or, in higher-torque designs, a segmented steel chain — that has to tolerate constant sideways squeezing.

questions.title: A block and tackle uses multiple pulleys and one continuous rope to lift a load. Which of these are true about how it multiplies force?
questions.description: Select every statement that is true.

options.text: The mechanical advantage roughly equals the number of rope segments actually supporting the moving pulley block attached to the load
To gain force, far more rope has to be pulled through than the distance the load actually rises
A block and tackle can multiply force with no tradeoff in how much rope has to be pulled
Adding more pulleys always increases mechanical advantage with zero increase in friction losses

questions.explanation: A block and tackle multiplies force by spreading the load's weight across several parallel rope segments instead of one, so each segment — and the hand pulling the free end — only has to support a fraction of the total weight. Count the number of rope segments actually holding up the moving block attached to the load, and that count is roughly the mechanical advantage, ignoring friction. That force multiplication is never free: because the total length of rope in the system is fixed, pulling the free end far enough to raise the load a given distance requires pulling in that many multiples of rope — a four-to-one system needs four metres of rope pulled through for every metre the load rises, trading distance and speed for force. Every extra pulley the rope runs over also adds a bit of friction, particularly with plain, non-ball-bearing sheaves, which is part of why a differential pulley — using a chain looped over a compound sprocket instead of separate rope segments — was developed to get large mechanical advantage along with a self-locking hold, without ever needing to tie the rope off.

questions.title: A screw thread is often described as 'an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder.' What does that description actually explain about turning a screw?

options.text: It explains why a small rotating force applied at the screw's head can produce a much larger straight-line force along its axis — the same trade a ramp makes between distance and force
It explains why screws have a round cross-section instead of a square one
It explains why screws must always be turned clockwise to tighten, in every culture and standard
It explains why longer screws are always structurally stronger than shorter ones

questions.explanation: Unroll a screw's thread and it really is a ramp: a shallow incline whose 'run' is the circumference the screw sweeps out per turn, and whose 'rise' is the thread pitch, how far the screw advances in that one turn. Walking a load up a shallow ramp lets a small push move it a large height, at the cost of walking a much longer distance than the height gained; turning a screw makes the identical trade, converting a modest rotating force applied at a large radius, the screwdriver or wrench, into a much larger force acting over the short distance of one thread pitch. A finer thread, with a smaller pitch, is a shallower ramp, trading more turns for more force per turn, which is exactly why fine-thread fasteners and lead screws can hold or move heavy loads with comparatively little twisting force. It is the same mechanical-advantage idea behind a wedge and an inclined plane, just wound helically instead of laid flat.

questions.title: A zipper's slider has no motor and grips no individual tooth by hand. As it is pulled along the zipper, what actually splits or re-meshes the two rows of teeth?

options.text: A Y-shaped channel inside the slider is wedge-shaped: moving one way it funnels the two rows of teeth together so they interlock, moving the other way it wedges between already-meshed teeth and forces them apart
Small magnets inside the slider attract or repel the metal teeth depending on the direction it is pulled
The slider spins rapidly as it travels, screwing the two rows of teeth together like a fine-pitched bolt
The fabric tape on either side of the teeth stretches and contracts to pull the teeth together or apart

questions.explanation: The zipper's teeth themselves do nothing active — every bit of work happens inside the slider's shape. Cut open a slider and its internal channel is a Y, splitting into two separate paths at one end and merging into a single path at the other. Pulled toward the merging end, that Y-shaped channel funnels the two rows of teeth inward until each tooth's hook interlocks with a tooth from the opposite row, the same way two zip-tied fingers interlace. Pulled the other way, the same wedge shape does the reverse: it is narrow enough at that end to insert itself between already-interlocked teeth, prying each pair apart as the slider passes through. No motor, no gripping, and no per-tooth action from the slider is involved — a single fixed wedge shape, moving through a chain of identical teeth, both closes and opens the whole zipper depending only on which direction it travels.

questions.title: A retractable click pen extends its tip on one press of the button and retracts it on the next, alternating every time, using only a spring and one button. What keeps track of whether the next press should extend or retract the tip?

options.text: A rotating cam follower with a star-shaped, notched tip turns slightly with every press, landing in a different notch each time, so it alternates between catching in an extended position and slipping free to retract
A tiny electronic counter inside the button remembers whether the last press extended or retracted the tip
Two separate springs of different strengths take turns winning, one press at a time
The pen has no memory of its state at all; every single press extends the tip, and it only retracts if the pen is shaken

questions.explanation: The 'memory' is entirely mechanical and geometric, not electrical. Pressing the button pushes down a plastic piston whose tip is cut into angled, star-like points, which presses against a matching fixed ring of points inside the pen's barrel. Each press pushes the piston's points fully down past the fixed points and lets it rotate slightly, twisted by the angled faces sliding past each other, before the spring pushes it back up partway. Because it rotated, it now lands on a different notch than before: one position catches on a small ledge partway up, holding the ink cartridge extended under spring tension; the next position has no ledge to catch, so the spring pushes the whole piston straight back up and retracts the tip. That alternation is why two distinct clicks are heard each cycle, one from the piston bottoming out and one from it catching or releasing, and why the mechanism keeps working after the pen has been taken apart and reassembled — there is no state stored anywhere except which notch the piston physically sits in.

questions.title: Pull several inches of steel tape out of a retractable tape measure and hold it out horizontally, unsupported. Why does the blade stay straight and rigid instead of flopping down under its own weight?

options.text: The blade is stamped with a slight concave, curved cross-section, and that curve resists bending far more than a flat strip of the same steel would
The blade is made from a much stiffer, heavier-gauge steel than a flat ruler of the same length would need
A separate stiffening spring is bonded to the underside of the blade for its first several inches
The blade is only rigid because of tension from the internal return spring still pulling on it

questions.explanation: This is a shape trick, not a material one. An ordinary sheet of paper flops immediately when held out flat, but curl it into a shallow trough and it can support its own weight standing out straight, because bending it now would also mean flattening or further curving that cross-section, which resists far more than the paper's flat bending stiffness alone. A tape measure's blade is stamped with exactly that shallow concave curve running along its length. As long as the blade stays straight, the curve holds and the strip behaves rigidly enough to reach across a room unsupported; push it too far past its rated 'standout' length, though, and the far end's own weight overcomes that resistance, the curve buckles flat or inverts, and the blade suddenly folds. The return spring inside the case is a completely separate mechanism — it only supplies the force that reels the tape back in and has nothing to do with why the extended blade stands out straight.
